claims.text: On October 17, 2026, DeepSeek pushed a checkpoint it called "a minor update" to its Flash endpoint.
Its own table puts the model at 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, against 74.0 and 51.8 for Claude Opus 5, at an advertised $0.15 per million input tokens.
Reposts collapsed this into "Opus 5 parity at 1/33rd the price."
As of 2026-10-17 no independent evaluator had scored 1017.
Opus 5 has been 'legacy' since Opus 5.5 shipped on 2026-09-22 at $4/$20 with Terminal-Bench 66.4.

DeepSeek's pricing page lists `deepseek-flash`, now served by "DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017", at $0.15 per million cache-miss input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens off-peak, doubling to $0.30 and $1.20 at peak[^3].
Cache hits cost $0.003 off-peak[^3].
The 1017 changelog says "the API calling method and pricing remain unchanged," so the price cut happened with the September V4.1-Flash release, not today[^4].
Claude Opus 5 lists at $5 input and $25 output, with cache reads at $0.50; Opus 5.5 lists at $4 and $20, with cache reads at $0.20[^12,10].
At 03:24 UTC on October 17, @teortaxesTex reported that the endpoint's `system_fingerprint` had changed to the MD5 of a build string naming `dsv41f_1017` with an FP8 KV cache[^24].
The headline numbers are real in the narrow sense: they appear on DeepSeek's own Hugging Face model card, under an MIT license, with a 1M-token context window[^1].
The 1017 card carries a single substantive footnote: "We use the Claude Code harness for Terminal-Bench 4.0 and the Mini-SWE-V2 harness for DeepSWE v1.1"[^1].
By contrast, the September V4.1-Flash card said all results "use the maximum effort setting (`reasoning_effort=100`)" with "N=8 samples per task on DeepSWE v1.1"[^5].
DeepSeek's own cost chart on the release page labels the 1017 points "training curve, eval step 196."
DeepSeek lists Opus 5 at 50.3 on Automation-Bench v1.0.6[^1].
Anthropic's own September launch post reports Opus 5 at 26.9% on AutomationBench, sourced from "Zapier's public leaderboard"[^10].
Zapier's live board has no standalone Opus 5 row; it shows Opus 5.5 at Max below 43%[^39].
DeepSWE v1.1 is maintained by Datacurve: 113 from-scratch tasks across 91 repositories in five languages, scored pass@1, with "all models run on mini-swe-agent for consistency"[^6,7,9].
Datacurve chose a single standard harness after a pilot in which mini-swe-agent "matches or beats every native harness at comparable token cost"[^8].
Its leaderboard, last updated September 22, puts Claude Opus 5 at max effort at **74% ±4%**, tied with GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 3.8 Flash at the top[^6].

In September DeepSeek showed how much the harness matters for its own model: the same V4.1-Flash checkpoint scored 74.2 on mini-SWE and 65.5 on OpenCode, an 8.7-point spread across eight scaffolds[^5].
Datacurve measured Opus 5 at max effort at **$11.84 per task**[^6].
DeepSeek's release chart puts 1017 at max effort at about $0.195 per DeepSWE task, down from about $0.495 for the September Flash.
Gemini 3.8 Flash already matched Opus 5's 74% at $2.36, a fifth of the cost, before DeepSeek shipped anything[^6].

The 51.8 matches the public leaderboard; Anthropic says the board, which uses "5 trials/task, Claude Code harness," reports Opus 5 at 51.8%, and its own setup "reproduces it at 52.3%, within noise"[^10].
The direction of that effect is not obvious: on Terminal-Bench 2.1 in September, Claude Code scored *lower* than DeepSeek's own harness for the same checkpoint, 88.0 vs 90.6[^5].
Artificial Analysis runs all 66 Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks on mini-swe-agent with three repeats[^15].
A secondary tracker of its results lists the September V4.1-Flash at 26.8, below DeepSeek's self-reported 31.2[^19].
The same tracker shows how strongly Opus 5's own score depends on effort: 34.9 at low, 44.9 at medium, 50.3 at high, 51.8 at max, and 53.9 at extra-high[^19].
Terminal-Bench 4.0 itself removed 8 tasks, fixed 19, and set a flat 8-hour agent timeout[^14].
@teortaxesTex, normally a DeepSeek bull, reported that 1017 is "massively faster than V4.1 Flash, but only up until it does 90% of the job," after which it needed close handholding[^22].
Thom Wolf of Hugging Face wrote that he was "curious to see how these numbers will hold up outside their own eval setup"[^23].
DeepSeek defines peak as "01:00 - 04:00 and 06:00 - 10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday, excluding Chinese public holidays," and says "off-peak rates are half of the peak rates"[^3].
OpenRouter lists 36 endpoints for `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`, with input prices from about $0.015 to $0.60[^26].
The Western cluster (Together, Fireworks, Nebius, BaseTen, Parasail) mostly charges $0.30 / $1.20, double the headline, and some US-region or "fast" endpoints charge $0.45–$0.60 input[^26].
Opus 5.5 has no such spread: every host, including Bedrock, Vertex and Azure, charges the $4 / $20 list price, with regional variants at $4.40 / $22[^27].
OpenRouter's October telemetry found cached tokens are "nearly nine in ten agentic tokens, but only about a third of the bill," with output around 1% of volume[^25].
It also found DeepSeek had the highest provider cache rate, about 96%[^25].
Heavy single-agent use can be more extreme still: one Claude Code user logged 5.09 billion cache-read tokens in 30 days against 3.89 million input-plus-output tokens[^43].
The counterpoint is availability: 99.47% uptime is about 3.9 hours of downtime a month, below "three nines"[^30].

Artificial Analysis records that the September V4.1-Flash at max effort "generated 250M tokens" running its Intelligence Index, "very verbose in comparison to the median of 130M," at $0.27 per task[^16].
Opus 5 at max used 140M tokens at $5.86 per task, and Opus 5.5 at max used 260M at $5.98[^17,18].

An ai.rs hands-on run of seven code-repair tasks, all solved by both checkpoints, found that "at equal effort, 1017 against its own September run thinks 18% less, answers 5% shorter and finishes 9% sooner"[^21].
Its claim that Opus 5.5 is "~40% cheaper than Opus 5 per task" is stated "at default settings"[^41,10].
The effort docs show the default dropped from `high` on Opus 5 to `medium` on Opus 5.5[^13].
DeepSeek's report says "the reported score of 46.4 was achieved using the Claude Code framework," and its own Terminus run gave 39.3[^31].
Vals measured 35.95 ±5.12[^32].
On SWE-bench Verified, DeepSeek's 73.1 came from "our internal framework," and Vals measured 67.6 ±2.1[^31,32].
V4-Pro's 80.6 became 77.4 ±1.9 at Vals[^33,34].

A May 2026 survey found that holding the model fixed and changing only the harness "raises Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 from 69.7% to 77.0%," and documents up to 15 points of scaffold-only variation on SWE-bench Verified[^35].
A September paper found "within-model scaffold ranges reach 29.8 percentage points, compared with the 8.8-point spread of the top thirty" on the SWE-bench board[^36].
DeepSeek's own chart shows 1017 at 72.6 for HIGH effort[^2].
Anthropic's own pricing page lists Opus 5 as legacy and Opus 5.5 at $4 input, $20 output and $0.20 cache read, 20% below Opus 5 on input and output and 60% below on cache reads[^12,10].
Artificial Analysis independently measured Opus 5.5 at 59.6 on its mini-swe-agent Terminal-Bench 4.0 run[^15], still about 17 points above 1017's self-reported score.

Vercel's AI Gateway reported that in July, Anthropic "collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume," with more than 80% of coding-agent spend, while DeepSeek held about a quarter of tokens and its spend share "barely moved"[^29].
OpenRouter said V4.1-Flash did "1T tokens in 24 hours" after launch, about 90% of them cache reads[^28].
A ByteDance Seed-led paper found "high average accuracy can coexist with systematic positional failures" in DeepSeek V4-family models.
It measured a 40.2-point best-to-worst phase gap on V4-Flash-Base, narrowing to about 4–6 points after post-training on V4.1-Flash[^37,38].
Section 1532 of the FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60) bars Department of Defense contractors from using AI "developed by" DeepSeek or High-Flyer in contract performance.
That ban has applied since January 17, 2026, and a compliance analysis reads it as covering self-hosted weights too[^40,46].
DeepSeek is not on the Commerce Entity List, although an interagency committee approved listing it[^45].

On DeepSWE-shaped work, where a test suite verifies each attempt, a cheap model can buy reliability by retrying: three 1017 attempts at about $0.20 each still cost about 5% of one Opus 5 attempt[^2,6].
